title: Hong Kong marks deadly fire anniversary with flowers, prayers and tears following government warning
html:
Mourners pay tributes to victims on the anniversary of the fire at Wang Fuk Court residential estate on Nov 26.

PHOTO: AP

AI generated

HONG KONG – Hong Kong residents on Nov 26 remembered the victims of the city’s deadliest fire in decades by offering flowers and prayers days after the government warned them to be cautious about commemorative activities and to avoid being exploited by people it said had ulterior motives.

The blaze engulfed seven high-rise buildings in Wang Fuk Court on Nov 26, 2025, killing 168 people and displacing thousands of others in a disaster unimaginable in the wealthy financial hub known for its safety and modernity.

A year on, many fire survivors were still grieving their losses despite life pushing them forward to adjust to their temporary housing, arrange funerals for their loved ones, clean up their belongings retrieved from charred homes and decide on resettlement plans.

At a park near the apartment complex in Tai Po in the north of Hong Kong, a steady stream of residents laid flowers, snacks and toys in tribute. Some returned to the familiar area and gazed at their old homes. Others wept.

Survivor YN Chi still remembered her escape from the complex a year ago, saying she would not be alive if she had left five minutes later. She feels frightened when she thinks about it.

“My greatest wish is to deliver the truth for those 168 victims,” she said. “They are truly innocent. It’s tragic.”

Performance artist Sanmu Chen laid some grass, saying humans are unlike grass and cannot be burnt or cut casually.

Beijing warns of attempts to stir up chaos

The tragedy is a sensitive issue in the Chinese territory, and not everyone feels free to speak about it.

As the first anniversary approached, Hong Kong’s No. 2 official, Eric Chan, said on Nov 20 that the government would allow all lawful commemorations but reminded residents to choose carefully what to take part in and not to be exploited by others to engage in disruptive acts.

Without identifying anyone, he said some people spoke plainly online that they hoped to use this opportunity to organise people to come out or carry out acts of disruption.

Echoing that, China’s Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office on Nov 24 urged vigilance against attempts to “use the disaster to stir up chaos”.

It said the government’s response demonstrated its decisive action in advancing reforms with efficiency and pragmatism.

Many residents have gradually emerged from the shadow of the tragedy and are grateful to the government and society, it added.

But Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, said the city government responded to the fire “by using Beijing’s tactics of shutting out the voices of the victims and promising an elusive accountability”.

Kai Chou, who studies in Tai Po, saw the flames from afar when the blaze broke out and, as a Hong Konger, he felt compelled to commemorate the victims of a tragedy that involved human-made mistakes.

He said it was not necessary for the government to urge residents to guard against those with ulterior motives and questioned if it was treating residents as “terrorists”.

“You made mistakes too, and yet even when we’re just trying to mourn, you still have to say things like this,” the 18-year-old Chou said.

Grace Chan, a non-Tai Po resident who offered a flower, told reporters with tears in her eyes that Hong Kong has changed and she could not digest it.

People offer flowers to victims on the anniversary of the fire at Wang Fuk Court residential estate.

PHOTO: BLOOMBERG

Hong Kong Journalists Association Chairperson Selina Cheng noted on Threads on Nov 25 that local journalists faced challenges in their anniversary coverage, saying a local television station had not broadcast its own report.

On the eve of the anniversary, the Hong Kong office of China’s Foreign Ministry e-mailed foreign news outlets, including The Associated Press, to provide information about the aftermath of the fire for reference.

It said the government was taking seriously the weak links in building maintenance and fire safety regulations exposed by the fire, and that it was committed to pursuing reform and investigations.

Religious commemorations are held

Beyond Tai Po, religious commemorations were held across the city, including a Mass that drew hundreds, including bereaved families, on Nov 25.

At a cathedral in Hong Kong’s downtown, the names of the 168 victims were read out one by one.

Jenny Lam, a pastor who lost three family members in the fire, said that on many sleepless nights, she thought about how those who remain should live on. She later realised they needed to live well.

“It’s not about forgetting our pain,” she said. “But rather... to continue experiencing the beauty of this world on their behalf.”

Phyllis Lo, whose mother died in the blaze, said she pondered where the victims lived and how their families would feel when she heard their names.

Lo had anticipated the government would hold commemoration activities, saying its apology was already late and doing so would show it was truly walking alongside them.

“There was disappointment, but I won’t place any expectations on it anymore,” Lo said.

Eric Chan, the official, earlier told a radio show that the authorities did not hold commemorations because other similar activities were already being organised.

An investigation found the blaze was likely caused by a lit cigarette and spread rapidly through non-fire-retardant scaffolding material. The report blamed faults in the complex’s renovation work and oversight deficiencies by several government departments.

Just a month ago, Hong Kong leader John Lee and officials bowed in apology, while his housing minister resigned.

Da Chung, a former Wang Fuk Court resident who attended the Mass, said that she was learning to make peace with the tragedy, but it was not easy for everyone.

She could feel the sadness of those who lost their families during the event.

“Their grief hangs in the air,” she said. AP
summary: Beyond Tai Po, religious commemorations were held across the city.
